Title Defense · Group DJANGO
BS CS – Data Science · FEU Tech

Fish provides food for our families and supports the livelihoods of coastal communities.

Behind every catch are fishers, vendors, and businesses that depend on a steady supply.

Can historical fisheries and environmental data help us anticipate when that supply may fall short?

00
Our proposed study
AquaTerra:
Forecasting Municipal Fish Landing Shortfalls and Estimating Gross Landing Value at Risk in Selected Philippine Coastal Provinces
Key terms · click
Municipal
Type of fishing operation, not a location: fishing without boats or with boats of 3 gross tons or less (PSA classification). Records are grouped by province.
Landings
Fish caught at sea and brought ashore. We measure the metric tons landed in each province during each quarter.
Quarter
Q1 Jan–Mar · Q2 Apr–Jun · Q3 Jul–Sep · Q4 Oct–Dec. PSA publishes the records quarterly.
Mangrove cover change
Historical increases or decreases in mangrove cover, derived from Landsat satellite imagery. Tested as a predictor; not assumed to cause anything.
Gross landing value at risk
Projected shortfall × matching historical first-sale price. Gross revenue tied to the missing landings, not income, profit or damage.
Fish provides food for our families and supports the livelihoods of coastal communities. [→] Behind every catch are fishers, vendors, and businesses that depend on a steady supply. [→] This makes understanding changes in fish landings important. Can historical fisheries and environmental data help us anticipate periods when that supply may fall short? [→] Good day, respected panelists. We are Group Django, and today we present our proposed study, 'AquaTerra: Forecasting Municipal Fish Landing Shortfalls and Estimating Gross Landing Value at Risk in Selected Philippine Coastal Provinces.' 'Municipal' describes the type of fishing operation: no boat, or a small boat of three gross tons or less; our records are grouped by province. 'Landings' means the catch brought ashore, in metric tons per province per quarter. (Click a key term to define it; press Q for the panel questions on the title.)
01
I · Background

Fish supports coastal livelihoods,
and national production is declining.

1 · Why it matters

Small-scale fisheries are an important source of rural livelihoods.

FAO (2024)

Municipal fisherfolk in Magallanes, Sorsogon faced income and food-security difficulties during COVID-19.

Dumilag et al. (2023)
2 · The decline
~45Mkg / year

average decline in Philippine capture fisheries production, 2010–2023

Oceana (2026) · national estimate, municipal + commercial; not province-level shortfalls
3 · Forecasting so far

A regional framework for commercial and marine municipal fisheries, comparing algorithms explained with SHAP.

Bokingkito et al. (2026)

Environmental predictors must be tested on unseen observations.

Holmes et al. (2021)
The concern  Can forecasts reliably flag shortfall periods and the province–category combinations with the most value at stake?
Fishing provides food, employment and income for Philippine coastal communities. FAO (2024) identifies small-scale fisheries as an important source of rural livelihoods. In the Philippine setting, Dumilag et al. (2023) documented income and food-security difficulties among municipal fisherfolk in Magallanes, Sorsogon during COVID-19. [→] The concern is reinforced by declining production. Oceana (2026) reports that Philippine capture fisheries production declined by about 45 million kilograms per year on average from 2010 to 2023, from about 2.6 to 1.9 million metric tons. This is a national estimate, municipal and commercial combined, separate from the province-level seasonal shortfalls we study. [→] Bokingkito et al. (2026) developed a regional forecasting framework covering commercial and marine municipal fisheries, comparing algorithms and explaining outputs with SHAP. Holmes et al. (2021) show environmental predictors should be tested for their contribution on unseen observations. [→] So the concern is whether forecasts can reliably identify shortfall periods and economically significant province–category combinations, using documented historical first-sale prices and sensitivity analysis.
02
II · Objectives

Four questions, five specific objectives.

General objective  Develop and evaluate AquaTerra, using Random Forest for predictor selection and GAMM for next-quarter municipal fish landing forecasts, then estimate supply shortfalls and gross landing value at risk to support planning in selected Philippine coastal provinces.
Research questions · click one
Specific objectives
1
Prepare
the dataset and seasonal benchmarks from quarterly landings, environmental information and historical reference prices
2
Forecast & evaluate
against a seasonal baseline with MAE, RMSE and MASE, including the added predictive value of mangrove history and prior typhoon exposure
3
Value exposure
calculate shortfalls, estimate gross landing value at risk, and rank province–category combinations
4
Validate & present
shortfall detection and rankings on unseen quarters, alternative price assumptions, planning dashboard
5
Seek collaboration
with DTI or a relevant fisheries agency to review data suitability and practical usefulness
The general objective is to develop and evaluate AquaTerra: Random Forest for predictor selection and GAMM for next-quarter forecasts, then estimate supply shortfalls and gross landing value at risk. We answer four questions [click each]. RQ1: what seasonal benchmarks identify shortfalls. RQ2: which predictors help GAMM, and do mangrove history and prior typhoon exposure improve accuracy. RQ3: what gross landing value goes with projected shortfalls. RQ4: how reliably are significant shortfalls identified on unseen quarters, and how price-sensitive are the rankings. Five specific objectives: prepare data and benchmarks; implement and evaluate the forecasting workflow; develop the economic exposure module; validate and present through a dashboard; and seek collaboration with DTI or a relevant fisheries agency.

What we cover, and what we don't claim.

Limitation · click an item to focus
Scope: forecasting marine municipal fish landings and assessing economic exposure in six Philippine coastal provinces (Palawan, Misamis Occidental, Negros Oriental, Tawi-Tawi, Zamboanga del Norte and Davao de Oro), using publicly accessible secondary data: PSA OpenSTAT, Landsat satellite imagery for mangrove cover, NASA IMERG, NOAA OISST and NOAA IBTrACS. Random Forest for predictor selection, then GAMM for next-quarter forecasts; compare with seasonal benchmarks, value shortfalls with historical reference prices, evaluate on later quarters, show results on a web dashboard, and seek consultation with DTI or a relevant fisheries agency. [→] Limitations: selected provinces and marine municipal categories only; no commercial, aquaculture or inland; no field monitoring. Next quarter only; gaps and delays may affect accuracy. We will not establish causal effects of mangrove change or typhoons. Gross landing value at risk uses historical prices, not income, profit or damage. The dashboard is a research prototype and adoption is not guaranteed.

3Time splitSplit by time, not at random.
Trainearliest quarters, e.g. 2002–2019. The model learns here.

Here is the whole pipeline, from raw data to pesos, in two slides. [Stage 1] We start with five public sources. PSA OpenSTAT gives quarterly landings, and the value records we use for prices, for each province and fish category. For example, Palawan snapper in the fourth quarter of 2025 was about 1,221 metric tons. Landsat satellite imagery gives mangrove cover: we derive the mangrove area for each province and year from the images. NASA IMERG gives rainfall. NOAA OISST gives sea surface temperature. NOAA IBTrACS gives typhoon tracks. [→ Stage 2] We line everything up into one table. Each row is one province, one fish category, one quarter. The columns are that quarter's landings, landings in the same quarter last year, the season, rainfall, sea temperature, mangrove area, recent typhoons, and the price. Price is only carried along for the money step at the end; it is never used to predict landings. [→ Stage 3] Then we split the rows by time, not at random. The earliest quarters train the model, the next quarters tune it, and the latest quarters are locked away as the test. The model never sees them until the final check. The years shown are an example.

[Stage 4] Only the training rows go into Random Forest. Random Forest ranks which columns help predict landings. It picks predictors; it does not make the forecast. Here the top four move on, and the weaker ones are dropped. Price is not a predictor; we only use it at the end. [→ Stage 5] GAMM builds the forecast by adding simple pieces: a seasonal curve, a smooth curve for each selected predictor, and a level shift for each province and fish category. Added together, they make the forecast line. [→ Stage 6] The output is next quarter's landings in metric tons for each province and fish category, with a range that shows the uncertainty. [→ Stage 7] Before we trust it, we check it on the locked test quarters against a simple baseline: the same quarter last year. We report MAE, RMSE and MASE. A MASE below one means we beat the seasonal-naive baseline. If we don't beat it, we say so. [→ Stage 8] Next, we compare each forecast with the usual level for that season, our benchmark. If the forecast is below it, the gap in tons is the projected shortfall. If it is above, there is no shortfall. [→ Stage 9] Finally, shortfall tons times the historical first-sale price gives pesos: gross landing value at risk. We rank the province–category combinations so planners know where to look first. This is gross value at stake, not lost income or profit. All numbers here are illustrative.
04
IV · Algorithm Justification · Random Forest

Many trees vote; importance ranks the predictors.

How it works
  1. Grow the forest. Each tree learns from a bootstrap sample of training quarters and a random subset of predictors.
  2. Rank predictors. Shuffle one predictor at a time; the bigger the error increase, the more important it is.
  3. Pass the top ones on. Only the selected predictors go into the GAMM.
Importance = predictive usefulness, not cause
Forest · one example quarter
ILLUSTRATIVE
Predictor importance
Pass top 4 to GAMM
Random Forest is an ensemble of decision trees. [→ Grow] Each tree learns from a bootstrap sample of the training quarters and a random subset of predictors; the forest averages the trees' predictions. [→ Rank] To rank predictors, we shuffle one predictor at a time and see how much the error increases; larger increases mean more useful predictors. [→ Pass] The top predictors go to the GAMM. Correlations alone can miss nonlinear patterns, which is why Nesslage et al. (2021) used Random Forest importance to guide GAMM construction. These numbers are illustrative. Importance means predictive usefulness, not cause.
04
IV · Algorithm Justification · GAMM

Smooth curves add up to the forecast.

Generalized Additive Mixed Model
Terms · click to add or remove
Random effects
level shifts per province & category
Landings (mt) · Province A · Category 1
ILLUSTRATIVE
dots = observed · line = model · ◆ next-quarter forecast
GAMM stands for Generalized Additive Mixed Model. [→] It adds a smooth seasonal curve for the quarter, [→] then smooth, possibly nonlinear curves for the predictors that Random Forest passed on, such as sea surface temperature, rainfall or lagged landings. [→] The 'mixed' part adds random effects, a level shift for each province and fish category, so groups can differ without fitting a separate model for each. [→] The sum gives the next-quarter forecast. All curves here are illustrative.

The workflow must beat the seasonal baseline on unseen quarters.

observedseasonal baseline = same quarter last yearRF → GAMM workflow
Error on test quarters
MAE: typical miss in mt · RMSE: punishes big misses · MASE < 1 beats the in-sample seasonal-naive error.
Selection and tuning stay inside training data. If the workflow doesn't beat the baseline, we report that.
We compare the complete workflow against a seasonal baseline: the observed landings from the same quarter of the previous year. [→] The test quarters are later quarters excluded from training and tuning; drag the slider to move the split, or play the rolling-origin evaluation. [→] MAE tells us the typical miss in metric tons, RMSE highlights larger mistakes, and MASE lets us compare across differently sized series. If the workflow adds little over the baseline, we would not recommend it for operational use. Values are illustrative.

IV · Algorithm Justification · Contribution test

Do mangrove history and typhoons improve the forecast?

Two models, same test quarters
Model Apast landings · seasonality · rainfall · SST
Model BModel A + mangrove history + prior typhoon exposure
Show
Possible result
Predictive, not causal: better accuracy ≠ mangroves cause landings
Test quarters · forecasts vs observed
ILLUSTRATIVE
To test predictive contribution we fit two models evaluated on the same unseen later quarters. [→] Model A uses past landings, seasonality, rainfall and SST. [→] Model B adds mangrove history and prior typhoon exposure. If Model B has lower MAE, RMSE and MASE, those predictors add predictive value. If not, we report that. Either way, better accuracy means predictive usefulness only. It does not prove mangroves or typhoons cause changes in landings. Values are illustrative.

IV · Algorithm Justification · Valuation

Shortfall × historical price = gross landing value at risk.

Pick a province × category

Gross landing value = Σ landings per fish category × matching historical first-sale price (same period, same province)
Shortfall

Value at risk

Exposure ranking · price sensitivity
First, what is gross landing value? For each province and quarter, we take how much of each fish category was landed, multiply it by the matching historical first-sale price for the same period and province, and add it up. [→] Value at risk works on the shortfall only. Our seasonal benchmark is the usual landing level for that province, fish category and quarter from earlier records. If the forecast is below it, the gap is the projected shortfall; if the forecast is above, the shortfall is zero. [→] We multiply the shortfall in tons, times 1,000 for kilograms, by that same historical first-sale price. That is the gross landing value at risk: the gross revenue tied to the missing landings. It is not profit and not household income loss. Where first-sale prices are missing, we use unit-value proxies. [→] Then we rank the province–category combinations. To defend the numbers, we switch price sources and move the price up or down, and check whether the ranking stays the same. Values here are illustrative.

V · Potential Clients

Who could plan with these estimates.

Primary potential users
LGUs & fisheries offices
identify projected shortfalls, prioritize monitoring, and inform assessments of potential assistance needs
BFAR
supplementary information for fisheries monitoring and planning in the covered provinces
DTI
economic exposure estimates to inform consultations and planning for fisheries-related enterprises
Fisherfolk associations & cooperatives
seasonal supply outlooks for collective marketing, delivery coordination and discussions with agencies
Traders, vendors & processors
projected shortfalls to inform sourcing, purchasing and inventory planning
As stated in our proposal, we will seek consultation with DTI or a relevant fisheries agency to assess data suitability and practical usefulness. Participation and future adoption are not guaranteed.
Our primary potential users are LGUs and fisheries offices, which may use provincial and fish-category forecasts to identify projected shortfalls, prioritize monitoring and inform assessments of assistance needs. [→] BFAR may use the findings as supplementary information for monitoring and planning. [→] DTI may use exposure estimates to inform consultations with fisheries-related enterprises. [→] Fisherfolk associations and cooperatives may use seasonal supply outlooks for marketing and delivery coordination. [→] Traders, vendors and processors may use projected shortfalls for sourcing and inventory planning. We will seek consultation with DTI or a relevant agency; participation and adoption are not guaranteed.

"How will you separate prediction from causation?"

1 · The test we run
Model Apast landings + seasonality
vs
Model BModel A + mangrove history + prior typhoon exposure
→
Unseen later quarterscompare MAE, RMSE, MASE
→
Better accuracy?= predictive usefulness only
2 · Why accuracy is not proof of cause

Other factors can move together with mangrove loss and also change recorded landings:

Fishing effortFuel pricesRegulationsReporting changes

Proving cause would need controlled or field studies, which are outside our scope.

3 · How we will word results
✓ "Mangrove history improves forecast accuracy for these provinces and quarters."
✕ "Mangrove loss causes lower landings."

Same rule for typhoon exposure, and for any predictor Random Forest ranks as important.

We test whether environmental information improves forecast accuracy. We compare a model with only past landings and seasonality against one with mangrove history and typhoon exposure added, both evaluated on unseen later quarters. [→] Better accuracy means predictive usefulness only. Fishing effort, fuel prices, regulations and reporting changes can move together with mangrove loss and also affect landings. Proving cause would need controlled or field studies, which are outside our scope. [→] So our results will say 'improves forecast accuracy', [→] never 'causes'.
